Cyclohexane — axial vs. equatorial H
Two matched models of the same chair ring, seen straight down the ring axis: space-filling (left) and ball-and-stick (right).
None — click any atom in the figure to light up one carbon together with its own axial (red) and equatorial (blue) hydrogen.
Drag to orbit: the flat-looking hexagon is really a chair. Red axial bonds stay parallel to the ring axis (3 up, 3 down); blue equatorial bonds splay out around the belt.

plan.chapterName: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 4: Organic Compounds: Cycloalkanes and Their Stereochemistry
plan.contextChunk: This figure looks straight down the axis of a chair-form cyclohexane ring in two matched models that color-code the two kinds of hydrogen position. On the left is a space-filling model: a compact dark gray core of ring carbons is surrounded by six large red spheres and six large blue spheres packed against one another, the red ones sitting toward the center of the disc and the blue ones fanning outward around the rim, the two colors alternating as the eye travels around the ring. A magenta arrow at the upper left points to a red sphere and is labeled "Axial"; a blue arrow at the top points to a blue sphere and is labeled "Equatorial". On the right the same view appears as a ball-and-stick model, the six dark gray carbons forming a hexagonal outline, with red spheres projecting from alternating carbons and blue spheres held outward from every carbon on thin pale rods. Separating the two positions by color rather than by perspective lets the reader count them directly, establishing that each ring carbon bears exactly one axial and one equatorial hydrogen and that each face carries three of each in alternating order.

elements: Chair-conformation cyclohexane ring of six dark-gray carbon atoms (alternating up/down puckering)
Six axial hydrogens, red, one per carbon, pointing parallel to the ring's C3 axis (three up, three down, alternating)
Six equatorial hydrogens, blue, one per carbon, splayed outward roughly in the ring plane

Space-filling (CPK) model panel: overlapping van der Waals spheres — compact dark-gray carbon core, red spheres clustered toward the disc center, large blue spheres fanning around the rim, red/blue alternating around the ring

Ball-and-stick model panel: small dark-gray carbon spheres forming a hexagonal outline, thin pale-gray/blue rods for C–C ring bonds and C–H bonds, red spheres on alternating carbons (axial, projecting toward viewer/away), blue spheres held outward from every carbon
Magenta arrow from upper-left pointing at a red sphere, with magenta text label 'Axial'
Blue arrow from top pointing at a blue rim sphere, with blue text label 'Equatorial'
Neutral white background, two side-by-side panels (space-filling left, ball-and-stick right)

interactions.teaches: Rotating away from the down-the-axis view reveals that the flat-looking hexagon is really a chair: the red axial hydrogens all stand parallel to the ring axis (alternating up and down) while the blue equatorial hydrogens splay outward near the ring's belt.

Clicking any ring carbon brightens that single carbon together with its own red axial and blue equatorial hydrogen, showing that both positions belong to the same carbon — every ring carbon carries exactly one of each.

interactions.label: Show hydrogens
interactions.teaches: Fading each set in and out makes the six axial (three up, three down, alternating) and six equatorial hydrogens individually countable, and shows they interleave one-for-one around the ring.

interactions.label: Model
interactions.teaches: Switching between the crowded space-filling view and the open ball-and-stick view shows they are the same molecule: the space-filling model shows how tightly the hydrogens pack, the ball-and-stick model exposes the bond directions hidden inside it.

demo_steps.title: Looking down the ring axis
demo_steps.narration: The space-filling model seen straight down the chair's axis: a dark gray carbon core, red axial hydrogens toward the center of the disc and big blue equatorial hydrogens around the rim, alternating as you travel around the ring.

demo_steps.title: Axial hydrogens only
demo_steps.narration: Hiding the blue hydrogens leaves six red axial hydrogens — three pointing up toward you and three pointing down away from you, strictly alternating around the six carbons.

demo_steps.title: Equatorial hydrogens only
demo_steps.narration: Now only the blue equatorial hydrogens remain, six of them fanning outward around the rim — again three tilted slightly up and three slightly down, alternating.

demo_steps.title: Open up the model
demo_steps.narration: The ball-and-stick view shows the same arrangement with the bonds visible. Click any carbon: its red axial and blue equatorial hydrogen light up together — both belong to that one carbon.

demo_steps.title: Compare the two models
demo_steps.narration: Side by side, the packed and open representations match position for position. Orbit to a side-on view to watch the axial bonds line up parallel to the ring axis while the equatorial bonds point out around the belt.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use 1 Å = 1 world unit. Cyclohexane chair, exact coordinates: six carbons at radius r = 1.46 from the ring axis (the axis = world +Y after the top-down camera, but build the ring in the XZ plane with pucker along Y), angles 0°,60°,...,300°, y = +0.25 for even-indexed carbons and y = −0.25 for odd-indexed (C–C 1.54 Å, C–C–C 111°). Axial C–H: length 1.09 along +Y from the up-puckered carbons and −Y from the down-puckered ones (exactly parallel to the ring axis). Equatorial C–H: length 1.09, directed radially outward from the axis and tilted ~19–20° opposite in sign to that carbon's axial direction (up-puckered carbon → equatorial tilts slightly down). Space-filling panel: van der Waals radii C 1.70, H 1.20, spheres interpenetrating so the gray carbon core is barely visible between the red/blue caps; red axial caps project toward/away from the viewer so they read as the inner ring of the disc, blue equatorial spheres form the outer rim — overall disc ≈ 6.5 units across. Ball-and-stick panel: C sphere r 0.36, H sphere r 0.24, rods r 0.075; ring spans ≈ 4.5 units across. Layout: in Side-by-side mode place the space-filling model centered at x = −4.6 and the ball-and-stick model at x = +4.6 (same size relationship as the source: space-filling disc visually a bit larger than the ball-and-stick hexagon); single-model modes center the model at origin. Colors: carbon dark slate gray #4B5053 with lighter specular highlight; axial hydrogen brick red #B8352A (space-filling) / #C0392B (ball-and-stick), with a glossy near-white specular dot upper-left of each sphere as in the source; equatorial hydrogen sky blue #46A8DC; bond rods pale gray-blue #C6D4DC with slightly darker outline; background white. Label 'Axial' in magenta #E0218A at upper-left with a magenta curved arrow pointing down-right onto an upper-left red sphere; label 'Equatorial' in blue #1C9AD6 at top with a blue arrow angled down-left onto the top blue rim sphere; labels attach to whichever model is leftmost/visible and hide when their hydrogen set is filtered out.
interactionPlan.notes: Three.js: MeshPhysicalMaterial (or MeshStandardMaterial with clearcoat-like low roughness ~0.25) plus one key directional light from the upper-left and a soft fill, to reproduce the glossy CPK highlight. Build each atom as a group so filtering just tweens material.opacity (transparent:true) and scale between 1 and 0 rather than removing meshes — keeps counts stable and the fade legible. Raycast only against carbon meshes (ball-and-stick mode) for the click interaction; on select, raise emissive on that carbon plus its paired axial and equatorial H and desaturate/dim all other atoms to ~35% opacity. Space-filling spheres need polygonOffset or slight radius jitter to avoid z-fighting at interpenetration seams; render with depthWrite true and no transparency unless a filter fade is active. Labels and arrows as CSS2DRenderer HTML overlays with SVG arrow paths so they stay crisp and can be pinned to atom screen positions during orbit (hide them once the camera tilts more than ~35° off the axis view). OrbitControls with damping, target at the ring centroid (or midpoint between panels in side-by-side), zoom limited so the figure keeps filling ~65% of the frame.

authoredContext:
As shown in the figure, each carbon atom in chair cyclohexane has one axial and one equatorial hydrogen. Furthermore, each side of the ring has three axial and three equatorial hydrogens in an alternating arrangement. For example, if the top side of the ring has axial hydrogens on carbons 1, 3, and 5, then it has equatorial hydrogens on carbons 2, 4, and 6. The reverse is true for the bottom side: carbons 1, 3, and 5 have equatorial hydrogens, but carbons 2, 4, and 6 have axial hydrogens (the figure).

Alternating axial and equatorial positions in chair cyclohexane, looking directly down the ring axis. Each carbon atom has one axial and one equatorial position, and each face has alternating axial and equatorial positions.

The space-filling model and ball and stick model of cyclohexane with alternate axial and equatorial positions, represented by red and blue spheres, respectively.

Note that we haven’t used the words cis and trans in this discussion of cyclohexane conformation. Two hydrogens on the same side of the ring are always cis, regardless of whether they’re axial or equatorial and regardless of whether they’re adjacent. Similarly, two hydrogens on opposite sides of the ring are always trans.

discrepancies: Annotation layout is mirrored: in the source both callout labels sit at the upper-LEFT with arrows sweeping down-right onto the molecule; the generated figure places 'Axial' above-right and 'Equatorial' far right, with arrows sweeping down-left.
The blue 'Equatorial' arrow tip stops in empty space to the right of the model rather than landing on a rim blue hydrogen sphere, weakening the annotation's meaning.

The source's second panel (ball-and-stick) is not shown by default; it is available only via the 'Ball-and-stick'/'Side-by-side' toggles, so the default view conveys only half of the two-panel source composition.
Red axial spheres in the generated space-filling model read slightly larger/more dominant than in the source, where the blue equatorial spheres are the visually largest rim features.
evaluation.notes: A chemically correct chair cyclohexane with proper axial (±ring-axis) and equatorial (~19.5° splay) hydrogens, viewed down the ring axis as in the source, with rich and pedagogically meaningful controls (model toggle, H filtering, atom picking, guided tour); main weaknesses are mirrored/loose callout arrow placement and the equatorial arrow not terminating on its target sphere.
action_items: Move the 'Axial' and 'Equatorial' labels to the upper-left as in the source and re-aim their curved arrows down-and-right onto a red axial sphere and a top blue equatorial sphere respectively.
Extend the equatorial arrow so its cone tip actually touches the surface of the targeted blue equatorial hydrogen.
Slightly rebalance sphere radii so the blue equatorial spheres visually dominate the rim as in the source, and confirm the dark gray carbon core reads as a continuous mass.
Consider defaulting the guided tour's first step (or adding a subtle hint) to reveal that the ball-and-stick companion panel exists behind the model toggle.

Raycast only against carbon meshes (ball-and-stick mode) for the click interaction; on select, raise emissive on that carbon plus its paired axial and equatorial H and desaturate/dim all other atoms to ~35% opacity. Space-filling spheres need polygonOffset or slight radius jitter to avoid z-fighting at interpenetration seams; render with depthWrite true and no transparency unless a filter fade is active. Labels and arrows as CSS2DRenderer HTML overlays with SVG arrow paths so they stay crisp and can be pinned to atom screen positions during orbit (hide them once the camera tilts more than ~35° off the axis view). OrbitControls with damping, target at the ring centroid (or midpoint between panels in side-by-side), zoom limited so the figure keeps filling ~65% of the frame.

plan.authoredPrompt: This figure looks straight down the axis of a chair-form cyclohexane ring in two matched models that color-code the two kinds of hydrogen position. On the left is a space-filling model: a compact dark gray core of ring carbons is surrounded by six large red spheres and six large blue spheres packed against one another, the red ones sitting toward the center of the disc and the blue ones fanning outward around the rim, the two colors alternating as the eye travels around the ring. A magenta arrow at the upper left points to a red sphere and is labeled "Axial"; a blue arrow at the top points to a blue sphere and is labeled "Equatorial". On the right the same view appears as a ball-and-stick model, the six dark gray carbons forming a hexagonal outline, with red spheres projecting from alternating carbons and blue spheres held outward from every carbon on thin pale rods. Separating the two positions by color rather than by perspective lets the reader count them directly, establishing that each ring carbon bears exactly one axial and one equatorial hydrogen and that each face carries three of each in alternating order.
plan.authoredInteractions:
- Click for selecting any ring carbon in the ball-and-stick model; its paired axial and equatorial hydrogens brighten together, clarifying that the two positions coexist on each carbon rather than belonging to separate molecules.
- Toggle axial only, equatorial only, and both: red and blue hydrogens fade in and out on both models, making the one-axial-one-equatorial pattern at every ring carbon countable.
plan.sourcePath: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 4: Organic Compounds: Cycloalkanes and Their Stereochemistry

discrepancies: Source is a two-panel figure (space-filling left, ball-and-stick right) shown simultaneously; the generated default shows only the space-filling model — the ball-and-stick and side-by-side layouts exist but are hidden behind the Model toggle / tour step 5.

In the space-filling model the axial hydrogens are given a smaller radius (1.16) than the equatorial hydrogens (1.28); both are hydrogens and should share a van der Waals radius — in the source the rim spheres only look larger because they are nearer/outer.

The magenta 'Axial' arrow tip lands on the outer left edge of the upper-left red sphere rather than clearly on its face as in the source, making the target slightly ambiguous where red and blue spheres abut.
Overall disc appears slightly more 'domed' (strong specular highlights, larger gray core gaps) than the flatter, more tightly packed hexagonal silhouette of the source space-filling model.
evaluation.notes: A faithful, well-built down-the-axis cyclohexane space-filling model with correct chair pucker, correct axial/equatorial geometry, matching colors and the two source callouts, backed by genuinely useful toggles (model type, H filter, per-carbon selection, 5-step tour); main shortfalls are that the source's two-panel side-by-side is not the default view and the axial/equatorial H radii differ artificially.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction structure are correct; remaining issues are implementation details (default to side-by-side layout, equalize hydrogen radii, fix arrow tip placement, flatten shading) rather than planning errors.

elements: Chair-conformation cyclohexane ring of six dark-gray carbon atoms (alternating up/down puckering)
Six axial hydrogens, red, one per carbon, pointing parallel to the ring's C3 axis (three up, three down, alternating)
Six equatorial hydrogens, blue, one per carbon, splayed outward roughly in the ring plane

Space-filling (CPK) model panel: overlapping van der Waals spheres — compact dark-gray carbon core, red spheres clustered toward the disc center, large blue spheres fanning around the rim, red/blue alternating around the ring

Ball-and-stick model panel: small dark-gray carbon spheres forming a hexagonal outline, thin pale-gray/blue rods for C–C ring bonds and C–H bonds, red spheres on alternating carbons (axial, projecting toward viewer/away), blue spheres held outward from every carbon
Magenta arrow from upper-left pointing at a red sphere, with magenta text label 'Axial'
Blue arrow from top pointing at a blue rim sphere, with blue text label 'Equatorial'
Neutral white background, two side-by-side panels (space-filling left, ball-and-stick right)

interactions.teaches: Rotating away from the down-the-axis view reveals that the flat-looking hexagon is really a chair: the red axial hydrogens all stand parallel to the ring axis (alternating up and down) while the blue equatorial hydrogens splay outward near the ring's belt.

Clicking any ring carbon brightens that single carbon together with its own red axial and blue equatorial hydrogen, showing that both positions belong to the same carbon — every ring carbon carries exactly one of each.

interactions.label: Show hydrogens
interactions.teaches: Fading each set in and out makes the six axial (three up, three down, alternating) and six equatorial hydrogens individually countable, and shows they interleave one-for-one around the ring.

interactions.label: Model
interactions.teaches: Switching between the crowded space-filling view and the open ball-and-stick view shows they are the same molecule: the space-filling model shows how tightly the hydrogens pack, the ball-and-stick model exposes the bond directions hidden inside it.

demo_steps.title: Looking down the ring axis
demo_steps.narration: The space-filling model seen straight down the chair's axis: a dark gray carbon core, red axial hydrogens toward the center of the disc and big blue equatorial hydrogens around the rim, alternating as you travel around the ring.

demo_steps.title: Axial hydrogens only
demo_steps.narration: Hiding the blue hydrogens leaves six red axial hydrogens — three pointing up toward you and three pointing down away from you, strictly alternating around the six carbons.

demo_steps.title: Equatorial hydrogens only
demo_steps.narration: Now only the blue equatorial hydrogens remain, six of them fanning outward around the rim — again three tilted slightly up and three slightly down, alternating.

demo_steps.title: Open up the model
demo_steps.narration: The ball-and-stick view shows the same arrangement with the bonds visible. Click any carbon: its red axial and blue equatorial hydrogen light up together — both belong to that one carbon.

demo_steps.title: Compare the two models
demo_steps.narration: Side by side, the packed and open representations match position for position. Orbit to a side-on view to watch the axial bonds line up parallel to the ring axis while the equatorial bonds point out around the belt.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use 1 Å = 1 world unit. Cyclohexane chair, exact coordinates: six carbons at radius r = 1.46 from the ring axis (the axis = world +Y after the top-down camera, but build the ring in the XZ plane with pucker along Y), angles 0°,60°,...,300°, y = +0.25 for even-indexed carbons and y = −0.25 for odd-indexed (C–C 1.54 Å, C–C–C 111°). Axial C–H: length 1.09 along +Y from the up-puckered carbons and −Y from the down-puckered ones (exactly parallel to the ring axis). Equatorial C–H: length 1.09, directed radially outward from the axis and tilted ~19–20° opposite in sign to that carbon's axial direction (up-puckered carbon → equatorial tilts slightly down). Space-filling panel: van der Waals radii C 1.70, H 1.20, spheres interpenetrating so the gray carbon core is barely visible between the red/blue caps; red axial caps project toward/away from the viewer so they read as the inner ring of the disc, blue equatorial spheres form the outer rim — overall disc ≈ 6.5 units across. Ball-and-stick panel: C sphere r 0.36, H sphere r 0.24, rods r 0.075; ring spans ≈ 4.5 units across. Layout: in Side-by-side mode place the space-filling model centered at x = −4.6 and the ball-and-stick model at x = +4.6 (same size relationship as the source: space-filling disc visually a bit larger than the ball-and-stick hexagon); single-model modes center the model at origin. Colors: carbon dark slate gray #4B5053 with lighter specular highlight; axial hydrogen brick red #B8352A (space-filling) / #C0392B (ball-and-stick), with a glossy near-white specular dot upper-left of each sphere as in the source; equatorial hydrogen sky blue #46A8DC; bond rods pale gray-blue #C6D4DC with slightly darker outline; background white. Label 'Axial' in magenta #E0218A at upper-left with a magenta curved arrow pointing down-right onto an upper-left red sphere; label 'Equatorial' in blue #1C9AD6 at top with a blue arrow angled down-left onto the top blue rim sphere; labels attach to whichever model is leftmost/visible and hide when their hydrogen set is filtered out.

discrepancies: The ball-and-stick panel is rendered noticeably smaller than the space-filling panel, whereas in the source the two models are roughly comparable in on-screen size, weakening the 'matched pair' reading.
Bond rods in the ball-and-stick model read as flat mid-gray, while the source uses pale blue-white highlighted sticks with a distinct two-tone/outlined look.

In the space-filling model the blue equatorial spheres in the source are fatter and more overlapping, forming a continuous rim; the generated rim spheres read as more separated lobes with more dark carbon core showing through.
Source red axial spheres sit tightly packed and nearly touching at the disc centre; the generated red spheres are slightly smaller/less crowded relative to the blue rim.
evaluation.notes: A faithful, well-composed reproduction of the two-panel axial/equatorial cyclohexane figure with correct chair geometry, correct color coding, correct callout arrows/labels, and a rich, conceptually meaningful interaction set (model toggle, H filter, atom picking, guided tour); main weaknesses are the undersized ball-and-stick panel and slightly off sphere packing/bond coloring relative to the print figure.
action_items: Scale up the ball-and-stick model (or reduce BS_EXT / increase its atom+rod radii) so both panels occupy comparable on-screen width as in the source.
Recolor the ball-and-stick rods toward the source's pale blue-white (#DCE8F0 with a lighter specular) and consider slightly thicker rods for the C–C bonds.

Increase the space-filling H sphere radius slightly (or reduce carbon radius) so the blue equatorial spheres overlap into a continuous rim and the red axial caps nearly touch, matching the printed packing.
Add a brief on-canvas panel caption (e.g. 'space-filling' / 'ball-and-stick') so the two models are self-identifying without reading the side panel.

feedback.rationale: Concept, structure, and interactions are correct; remaining issues are concrete rendering fixes (panel scaling, rod color, sphere radii, panel captions) that belong to the generator.
